report.answer_text:
What the first images showed (released June 23, 2025)
The NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory team revealed the first images on June 23, 2025.[1] The "First Look" gallery included "The Cosmic Treasure Chest," "A Swarm of New Asteroids," "Rhythms in the Stars," and the Trifid and Lagoon Nebulae.[1]
Virgo Cluster: One image shows the Virgo galaxy cluster. It contains about 10 million galaxies, roughly 0.05% of the ~20 billion galaxies Rubin will capture over ten years.[2]
Trifid and Lagoon Nebulae: This image combines 678 images taken in about 7 hours of observing time.[3]
Asteroids and variable objects: The release also covered thousands of new asteroids[4], along with videos of a changing sky.
Scale: The images came from only about 10 hours of observations.[5] Each would need about 400 HD televisions to display at full detail.[5] They were taken with a 3,200-megapixel camera[4] on the 8.4-meter Simonyi Survey Telescope[6], in Chile.
The survey: the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST)
Rubin's main mission is the LSST, a decade-long survey that repeatedly scans the southern night sky. It builds an ultra-wide, ultra-high-definition time-lapse record of the universe.[6]
It will image the entire southern sky every three to four days and produce about 20 terabytes of data each night.[7]
Its science goals include dark matter and dark energy, distant galaxies, supernovae, and active galactic nuclei with supermassive black holes.[2] It is also expected to discover millions of new asteroids within the first two years.[3]
The sources I found from 2025 expected the LSST to start in late 2025. I didn't check whether it has formally begun.
